meta.title: Who really said "This Just Shows What God Could Do If He Had Money"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Alexander Woollcott. Quote Investigator traces this floating estate quip to a 1929 Peter Fleming letter; Woollcott’s credit is Moss Hart’s 1959 memoir.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'This Just Shows What God Could Do If He Had Money'?
meta.ogDescription: A floating quip, not Woollcott's line. Earliest known use: Peter Fleming's letter of 29 Sept 1929. The estate anecdote first credited Wolcott Gibbs in 1940.

answer.label: Not Alexander Woollcott — earliest traced to Peter Fleming
answer.authorDates: 1907–1971 · British travel writer · Quote Investigator’s leading candidate, not a settled attribution
answer.sourceLine: This is a floating quip, not a Woollcott line. Quote Investigator ↗ locates its earliest known use in a letter Peter Fleming wrote on 29 September 1929 — about Long Island, not about anybody’s house — and its earliest publication in The Fortnightly Review of June 1933, where the writer credited only an unnamed wag. The Woollcott credit surfaces once, in Moss Hart’s memoir Act One (1959), in different wording, sixteen years after Woollcott’s death; the earlier estate version, printed by Frank Case in 1940, puts the line in the mouth of a different man with a confusingly similar name, Wolcott Gibbs.

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from

docMeta.dd: Letter, Peter Fleming to Rupert Hart-Davis, 29 September 1929, from the Piping Rock Club, Locust Valley
Peter Fleming: A Biography (Duff Hart-Davis, 1974), p. 67
The Fortnightly Review, London, June 1933 — Ivor Brown, crediting only an unnamed wag

source.excerpt: Finally, returning to the house after inspection of the domain, the owner points to a magnificent elm growing in the terrace just outside the library window. “See that tree? That tree stood for fifty years or more on top of that hill over there. I had it moved down here so on pleasant mornings I can do my work out here in its shade.” “That just shows what God could do if he had money,” says Gibbs.
trail: 1929 — the earliest known use, and it is not about a house. Peter Fleming wrote from Long Island that the place “represents the Americans’ idea of what God would have done with Nature if he’d had the money.” The letter is dated 29 September 1929 and is printed in Duff Hart-Davis’s biography of Fleming; the chronology is assembled by Quote Investigator ↗.

1933 — first in print, with nobody’s name on it. Quote Investigator’s earliest published evidence is a June 1933 article by the drama critic Ivor Brown in the London periodical The Fortnightly Review, which used the line — “It’s what God would have done with Nature, if He had had the money” — and credited an unnamed wag ↗.

1940 — the joke shrinks to one estate, and gets a speaker. Frank Case, the Algonquin proprietor, printed the transplanted-elm anecdote in Do Not Disturb and gave the punchline to Wolcott Gibbs of The New Yorker ↗.

1959 — Woollcott’s name is attached, posthumously. Moss Hart’s Act One (Random House, 1959) ↗ credits “the late Alexander Woollcott” with “Just what God would have done if He had the money” — a different wording, published sixteen years after Woollcott died in 1943 and twenty-six years after the line was already in print without him.
source.excerptNote: This is the earliest printing of the estate anecdote in essentially the popular wording — and the speaker is Wolcott Gibbs, not Alexander Woollcott. The joke itself is older: Peter Fleming used it about Long Island as a whole in a letter four years before it first reached print, anonymously, in 1933.

source.rightsNote: No public-domain claim is made here, because the wording cannot be tied to a specific work. The earliest located instance is an unpublished 1929 letter that did not reach print until Duff Hart-Davis’s biography of Peter Fleming in 1974, and every documented printing of the line — The Fortnightly Review (1933), Frank Case’s Do Not Disturb (1940), Moss Hart’s Act One (1959) — falls after 1931 and belongs to its own author and publisher. The quip as a floating one-liner has no identifiable rights holder; the books that contain it do.

author.name: Peter Fleming
author.heading: So who was Peter Fleming?
author.metaLine: 1907–1971 · British travel writer, Times correspondent & elder brother of Ian Fleming
author.bio: Peter Fleming was a British travel writer, journalist and adventurer best known for Brazilian Adventure (1933) and News from Tartary (1936), and for his work as a special correspondent for The Times. He was the elder brother of Ian Fleming, and wrote essays for The Spectator under the pen name “Strix.” His 1929 letter from Long Island is the earliest instance of this joke anyone has located — though as Quote Investigator is careful to say, he either crafted the remark or was relaying a witticism already circulating on Long Island.

copyAttribution: "This just shows what God could do if he had money." — not Alexander Woollcott. A floating quip with no settled author: the earliest known use is Peter Fleming's letter of 29 September 1929 (printed in Duff Hart-Davis, Peter Fleming: A Biography, 1974), and the earliest publication is an anonymous credit in The Fortnightly Review, June 1933. Frank Case's Do Not Disturb (1940) gives the estate version to Wolcott Gibbs; the Woollcott credit appears only in Moss Hart's Act One (1959), in different wording. Chronology via Quote Investigator.

misattribution.heading: Five men have been handed this line
misattribution.intro: None of the credits below is supported by a contemporary record of the speaker saying it. Each is a later retelling that fixed the joke to a particular house and a particular guest — and the joke is older than all of them.

items.why: The only source is Moss Hart’s Act One (1959), where Hart writes that after he built needless wings on his country house and planted thousands of trees, “the late Alexander Woollcott was prompted to remark a little contemptuously, ‘Just what God would have done if He had the money.’” That is not the popular wording, it is a recollection published sixteen years after Woollcott’s death in 1943 ↗, and the joke was already in print — unattributed — by 1933. The Woollcott form still circulates locally: the Michener Art Museum’s Bucks County artists database ↗ repeats it about Hart’s Fairview Farm in Solebury Township.

Nineteen years before Hart’s memoir, Algonquin proprietor Frank Case gave the estate anecdote to the New Yorker writer Wolcott Gibbs in Do Not Disturb (1940) — and that version carries almost exactly the popular wording. Quote Investigator flags the obvious hazard, noting that misattributions are generated when credit shifts between people with similar names, “e.g., between Wolcott Gibbs and Alexander Woollcott” ↗. Gibbs is the earlier claimant, but he is not the originator either.

A 1946 Boston Herald item put the remark at Moss Hart’s farm and gave it to the New York Times drama critic Brooks Atkinson, in the form “This shows what God could do if He only had money” — same house, different guest, per Quote Investigator’s chronology ↗.

A Dallas columnist in 1964 reported Kitty Carlisle’s version of the story, which credited Hart’s writing partner George S. Kaufman: “God would have done the same if he had had the money” — recorded by Quote Investigator ↗.

Ken Murray’s The Golden Days of San Simeon (1971) reported a rumour that Shaw said it at Hearst’s estate. Quote Investigator’s verdict is blunt: that version “currently has very weak support and is probably apocryphal” ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Quote Investigator’s conclusion is the honest answer: “Peter Fleming is the leading candidate for crafter of this quip by 1929… the quipster was probably Wolcott Gibbs or Alexander Woollcott” ↗ — leading candidate and probably, not proven.

context.heading: Why this joke keeps changing owners
lead: The line is built to travel. It needs only a rich man, a landscape he has improved, and a guest sharp enough to say the obvious thing — so it re-attaches itself to whatever estate and whatever wit are in front of the teller. Fleming aimed it at the whole of Long Island in 1929. By 1933 The Fortnightly Review was using it about Herbert Beerbohm Tree’s spectacular Shakespeare productions and crediting nobody. By 1940 it had narrowed to a single house, a single transplanted elm, and a single named speaker.

Once it narrowed, the names began to rotate. Frank Case gave it to Wolcott Gibbs; a 1946 newspaper gave it to Brooks Atkinson; Moss Hart gave it to Alexander Woollcott; a 1964 columnist relayed Kitty Carlisle’s version crediting George S. Kaufman; and by 1971 it had been handed to George Bernard Shaw standing in Hearst’s San Simeon. Every one of those men is plausible, which is exactly the problem — a quip that fits any wit will eventually be attributed to all of them.
context.detailsSummary: The two names that keep swapping
detailsBody: Wolcott Gibbs and Alexander Woollcott overlapped at The New Yorker, and Quote Investigator names this pairing outright as an example of how credit drifts between people with similar names. Wikipedia records that the two were frequently confused or assumed to be related ↗ despite not being relatives — and that Gibbs privately loathed Woollcott, calling him one of the most dreadful writers who ever existed.

Moss Hart’s own telling is worth reading in full, because it is not a boast. He is describing his own extravagance: he had built needless wings on his country house and planted thousands of trees, and records that “the late Alexander Woollcott was prompted to remark a little contemptuously” — the joke was at Hart’s expense, which is one reason it has stuck to his farm ever since.
context.pull: A joke that fits any estate will sooner or later be credited to every wit who ever visited one.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator traces the quip to a Peter Fleming letter dated 29 September 1929 (written from the Piping Rock Club, Locust Valley, and printed in Duff Hart-Davis's 1974 biography, p. 67) and concludes Fleming is the leading candidate for crafting it by 1929.

Quote Investigator states its earliest published evidence is June 1933 in the London periodical The Fortnightly Review, in an article by drama critic Ivor Brown, who credited an unnamed wag: 'It's what God would have done with Nature, if He had had the money'.

Quote Investigator reproduces the passage from Frank Case's Do Not Disturb (Frederick A. Stokes Company, 1940, p. 276) in which, after the owner shows off a transplanted elm, 'That just shows what God could do if he had money,' says Gibbs.

Quote Investigator reproduces Moss Hart's Act One (Random House, 1959, pp. 27-28): 'I have built needless wings on my house in the country and planted thousands of trees on my land, so that the late Alexander Woollcott was prompted to remark a little contemptuously, "Just what God would have done if He had the money."'

Quote Investigator notes that misattributions are generated when credit shifts between people with similar names, 'e.g., between Wolcott Gibbs and Alexander Woollcott', and concludes the George Bernard Shaw / San Simeon version 'currently has very weak support and is probably apocryphal'.

Quote Investigator's chronology also records a 1946 Boston Herald item crediting Brooks Atkinson at Moss Hart's farm ('This shows what God could do if He only had money') and a 1964 Dallas column relaying Kitty Carlisle's version crediting George S. Kaufman ('God would have done the same if he had had the money'), plus Ken Murray's The Golden Days of San Simeon (1971) for the Shaw version.

Alexander Woollcott was born 19 January 1887 and died 23 January 1943; he was drama critic for The New York Times, a member of the Algonquin Round Table, and the inspiration for Sheridan Whiteside in Kaufman and Hart's The Man Who Came to Dinner.

Peter Fleming (31 May 1907 - 18 August 1971) was a British travel writer, journalist and Times special correspondent, elder brother of Ian Fleming; Duff Hart-Davis's Peter Fleming: A Biography was published by Jonathan Cape in 1974.

Wolcott Gibbs (1902-1958) was a New Yorker writer who became the magazine's theatre critic in 1938; he and Alexander Woollcott were frequently confused or assumed to be related despite not being relatives, and Gibbs strongly disliked Woollcott.
The Internet Archive holds a borrowable copy of Moss Hart's Act One: An Autobiography, New York: Random House, 1959.
The Internet Archive holds a borrowable copy of Duff Hart-Davis's Peter Fleming: A Biography (Oxford University Press, 1987 printing).

The Michener Art Museum's Bucks County Artists Database records that Moss Hart bought Fairview Farm in Solebury Township and that Woollcott remarked of his improvements, 'Just what God would have done if He had the money.'

NEGATIVE CHECK - Wikiquote's Alexander Woollcott page lists this quotation (in either its Quotes or Misattributed section). It does not; nothing about God and money appears there, so the page is not cited as support.
